title: Everyone's a Learning Scientist These Days... Apparently.
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner, a career researcher in learning and instruction, objects to the spread of the label 'learning scientist' among people who read and summarise research without conducting it. Using the Science Council's definition of science as a systematic, evidence-based enterprise, he argues that communicating research and doing research are different activities. He accepts that good science communicators are valuable, and names several. His complaint is that 'learning science' has become an elastic brand, citing a scoping review that found 43 definitions across 50 documents. When the label substitutes for evidence, authority detaches from rigour and teachers are sold certainty the research does not give. He asks that people call themselves learning scientists, science communicators, educational consultants or edfluencers according to what they actually do.
points: Reading, explaining or presenting research is not doing research; a learning scientist is someone who contributes original inquiry into how people learn.
Good science communicators, some of whom never ran a study, are necessary, and Kirschner has no quarrel with them.
'Learning science' has become so elastic that a scoping review found 43 definitions across 50 documents, so the term distinguishes nothing.
When science becomes a brand, trust follows the label instead of the evidence, and hedged findings are traded for 'five scientifically proven strategies' slogans.
He proposes honest titles (learning scientist, science communicator or research translator, educational consultant, edfluencer) matched to what a person does.
quotes: Reading research, explaining research, or giving workshops or keynotes about research isn’t doing research.

What bothers me is that communicating science and doing science are increasingly being treated as though they’re the same, and that the distinction between a scientist and someone who talks about science seems to have all but disappeared.
It has become so elastic that it can mean almost anything and a label that includes virtually everything ultimately distinguishes nothing.
More seriously, when ‘science’ becomes a brand, scientific authority becomes detached from scientific evidence.
Apparently, “Research suggests that this may work under certain conditions” doesn’t sell quite as well as “Five scientifically proven strategies that will transform your teaching.

The problem isn’t that edfluencers are wrong or that scientists are right, but that influencing an audience, communicating research done by others, and conducting scientific research are fundamentally different activities.
Knowing about learning doesn’t make you a learning scientist, any more than knowing about medicine makes you a medical scientist.
